questions.q: Why is { message: "task created", taskId: 7, userId: "ada" } easier to use later than the sentence "Task 7 created by ada"?
questions.explain: A structured entry is a record: a short fixed message plus named fields. You can search userId === "ada" exactly, like a database column. With sentences you must guess every way the text could be worded.
options: It is shorter, so the log file uses less disk space
Log tools can filter and count by named fields, without guessing how each sentence was worded
Sentences cannot contain numbers in a log
Only objects can be printed with console.log

questions.q: In a structured log entry, what is the metadata?
questions.explain: The message says what happened ("task created") and stays the same every time. The details that change (taskId, userId) go into metadata fields.
options: The time and the level of the entry
The name of the file that wrote the entry
The details, stored in separate named fields next to a short fixed message
The full sentence that describes what happened

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two records have the message "task created", from ada and linus. Two records have taskId 7. Because the message is fixed and the details are fields, these searches are exact.
options:
[ 'ada', 'linus' ]
2

[ 'ada', 'ada', 'linus' ]
2

[ 'ada', 'linus' ]
1

questions.q: A logger has a formatter and one or more transports. What does a transport do?
questions.explain: The formatter turns an entry into text. The transport receives the entry and sends the text somewhere. A transport can be a plain function.
options: It decides which levels are written
It turns an entry into readable text or JSON
It sends the formatted entry somewhere: the terminal, a file or a log service
It hides passwords before the entry is written

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The text formatter writes the level, the logger name, the message, then the metadata as key=value pairs. A value with a space gets quotes, so title="Buy milk" stays one field.
options: [INFO] [task-api] task created taskId=7 title="Buy milk"
[INFO] [task-api] task created taskId=7 title=Buy milk
[task-api] [INFO] task created taskId=7 title="Buy milk"
[INFO] task created { taskId: 7, title: 'Buy milk' }

questions.q: This transport prints fields of the entry instead of the formatted text. What does it print?
questions.explain: entry.levelName is the lower-case name "warn" (the number is in entry.level). entry.metadata is a real object, so console.log prints it as an object, not as key=value text.
options: warn task-api { durationMs: 840 }
WARN task-api { durationMs: 840 }
warn task-api durationMs=840
2 task-api { durationMs: 840 }

questions.q: Which list shows the six log levels from most to least serious?
questions.explain: fatal means the process cannot continue. trace is the most detailed step-by-step information. warn (unusual but handled) is more serious than info (normal events).
options: fatal, error, warn, info, debug, trace
error, fatal, warn, info, trace, debug
trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal
fatal, error, info, warn, debug, trace

questions.q: The default threshold is info. What does this print?
questions.explain: With the threshold info, the debug entry is dropped. After setLevel(LoggerLevel.WARN), the logger only writes warn and more serious, so "task updated" is dropped but the error is written.
options:
[INFO] [task-api] task created
[ERROR] [task-api] could not save task

[DEBUG] [task-api] cache miss
[INFO] [task-api] task created
[ERROR] [task-api] could not save task

[INFO] [task-api] task created
[INFO] [task-api] task updated
[ERROR] [task-api] could not save task
[INFO] [task-api] task created

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With the threshold debug, the logger writes debug and everything more serious, like info. trace is less serious than debug, so it is still dropped.
options:
[DEBUG] [worker] job picked jobId=3
[INFO] [worker] job done jobId=3

[TRACE] [worker] step 1
[DEBUG] [worker] job picked jobId=3
[INFO] [worker] job done jobId=3
[INFO] [worker] job done jobId=3
[DEBUG] [worker] job picked jobId=3

questions.q: A database query took 2 seconds, but the request still worked. Which level fits best?
questions.explain: warn is for something unusual that was handled. error is for something that failed and should have worked, and fatal means the process cannot continue.
options: error
warn
fatal
trace

questions.q: Where should the Task API get its log level from?
questions.explain: The level belongs in configuration, so you can change it per environment without changing code. Never let a client choose it, and don't log everything at trace: the real problems drown in noise.
options: A constant in each service file
Configuration: a LOG_LEVEL environment variable
The client, through a query parameter such as ?log=debug
It should always be trace, so nothing is lost

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A child logger gets its own name and adds its metadata to the parent's. So the line carries the parent's version, the child's component, and the entry's own pool.
options: [INFO] [task-api.db] connected version=0.1.0 component=db pool=10
[INFO] [task-api.db] connected component=db pool=10
[INFO] [task-api] connected version=0.1.0 component=db pool=10
[INFO] [task-api.db] connected pool=10

questions.q: Inside a service you need a logger. What does the lesson tell you to do?
questions.explain: A logger made with createLogger inside a service ignores every setting of the main one: level, formatter, transports. A child shares them and adds its own name and metadata.
options: Call createLogger inside the service, so it has its own settings
Use console.log, because services should not know about the logger
Create a child of the main logger when the app starts and pass it into the service
Import the main logger and change its name inside the service

questions.q: Why put a request id on every log line a request writes?
questions.explain: A server handles many users at once, so their lines interleave. With the same id on every line of one request, you can pull out exactly that request's lines.
options: It makes the log lines sort by time
It stops the client from sending the same request twice
The lines of many requests are mixed together; one search for the id shows one request's whole story
The log store refuses lines without an id

questions.q: Several services pass the same id along, so one user action can be followed through all of them. What is this id called?
questions.explain: A request id follows one request in one service. When the same id is passed from service to service, it is called a correlation id.
options: A session id
A correlation id
A tenant id
A log level

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: withContext returns a new logger that adds the context to every entry. The original logger is unchanged, so its line has no request id.
options:
[INFO] [task-api] task created requestId=req-41 userId=ada taskId=7
[INFO] [task-api] no request here

[INFO] [task-api] task created taskId=7
[INFO] [task-api] no request here

[INFO] [task-api] task created requestId=req-41 userId=ada taskId=7
[INFO] [task-api] no request here requestId=req-41 userId=ada

[INFO] [req-41] task created userId=ada taskId=7
[INFO] [task-api] no request here

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The context travels into child loggers of the scoped logger. So the database line of this request still carries requestId=req-8.
options: [INFO] [task-api.db] row inserted requestId=req-8 table=tasks
[INFO] [task-api.db] row inserted table=tasks
[INFO] [task-api] row inserted requestId=req-8 table=tasks
[INFO] [task-api.db] row inserted requestId=req-8

questions.q: A client sends its own x-request-id header. What is the safe way to handle it?
questions.explain: The header comes from the client, so anyone can choose it and mix fake lines into another request's story. Your own id (for example from randomUUID()) is the one you trust. The client's value is just extra, checked data.
options: Use it as the request id, so the client and server share one id
Reject every request that has the header
Create your own id; if you keep the client's value, log it as a separate field after checking its length and characters
Use it only when it looks like a UUID, without any other checks

questions.q: When something throws, why should you log the error object and not only error.message?
questions.explain: The stack trace is the list of function calls that led to the error. Its first frame points at the line where the error was created: that is where you start looking.
options: The message is always empty
The object carries the error's name and its stack trace, which shows where the error was created
Logging the object sends it to the client too
The logger refuses strings as errors

questions.q: This transport prints fields of the entry. What does it print?
questions.explain: logError(logger, error, message, metadata) writes an error entry with the error attached. entry.error keeps the error's real name and message, while the entry's own message is "request failed".
options: error TypeError title must be a string { status: 500 }
error Error title must be a string { status: 500 }
warn TypeError title must be a string { status: 500 }
error TypeError request failed { status: 500 }

questions.q: A client asks for a task that does not exist, and your API answers 404. How should you log it?
questions.explain: A 4xx is not a failure of your server. Keep error for 5xx, the failures you must fix. If every 404 is an error, the real errors drown.
options: As error with a stack trace, so nothing is missed
As warn (or info) without a stack trace, because it is the client's mistake
As fatal, because a task is missing
Don't log it, and don't count it anywhere

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: NotFoundError is a BaseError with statusCode 404, so it is logged as a warning. A plain Error is not a BaseError, so it counts as 500 and is logged as an error.
options:
[WARN] [task-api] request rejected status=404
[ERROR] [task-api] request failed status=500

[ERROR] [task-api] request failed status=404
[ERROR] [task-api] request failed status=500

[WARN] [task-api] request rejected status=404
[WARN] [task-api] request rejected status=500

[WARN] [task-api] request rejected status=500
[ERROR] [task-api] request failed status=500

questions.q: A save fails in the repository. Where should the error be logged?
questions.explain: Logging the same error in every layer makes three entries for one problem. Let it travel up and log it once, in the request wrapper, which also knows the request id.
options: In the repository, the service and the handler, so every layer sees it
Once, in the request wrapper, where the request id is also available
Nowhere: the client gets the error, that is enough
In the repository only, and then the error is swallowed

questions.q: A database error happens while handling a request. What should the client receive?
questions.explain: Error details can reveal how your system works, file paths or data. They belong in the log. The client gets a status like 500 and a safe message.
options: The error message and stack trace, so they can report it
The SQL that failed
The status and a safe message; the details go only to the log
Nothing at all: close the connection

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Redaction is on by default. A field whose name looks secret, like password, is replaced with [REDACTED] before any formatter or transport sees it. userId is not secret, so it stays.
options: [INFO] [task-api] login userId=ada password=[REDACTED]
[INFO] [task-api] login userId=ada password=hunter2
[INFO] [task-api] login userId=ada
[INFO] [task-api] login userId=[REDACTED] password=[REDACTED]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Redaction also works inside nested objects: authorization is hidden, while accept is kept. The transport already receives the redacted metadata. The debug entry was dropped by the level check.
options: { authorization: '[REDACTED]', accept: 'application/json' }
{ authorization: 'Bearer abc.def', accept: 'application/json' }
{ accept: 'application/json' }
[REDACTED]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: redact.keys adds names to the default list. So email is hidden because you added it, and token is still hidden by default.
options: [INFO] [task-api] signup userId=ada email=[REDACTED] token=[REDACTED]
[INFO] [task-api] signup userId=ada email=[REDACTED] token=t-1
[INFO] [task-api] signup userId=ada email=ada@example.com token=[REDACTED]
[INFO] [task-api] signup userId=ada email=[REDACTED]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Redaction works on field names only. The token was glued into the message text, so it leaked. Never build messages from outside values: keep the message fixed, like "token issued", and leave the token out.
options: [INFO] [task-api] token issued: abc123
[INFO] [task-api] token issued: [REDACTED]
[INFO] [task-api] [REDACTED]
[INFO] [task-api] token issued: token=[REDACTED]

questions.q: Which of these lines leaks a secret into the logs?
questions.explain: The password field is redacted by name. But a value glued into the message text is never redacted, so the template string leaks it. The last option names the reason, not the password itself.
options: log.info("login", { user, password })
log.info(`login with password ${password}`)
log.info("login", { userId: user.id })
log.warn("login failed", { userId: user.id, reason: "bad password" })

questions.q: A task title contains a newline. What does this print?
questions.explain: A newline in a value is an attempt to fake a second log line: log injection. The formatter escapes it to \n, so everything stays inside one entry.
options: [INFO] [task-api] task created title="Milk\n[ERROR] fake"

[INFO] [task-api] task created title="Milk
[ERROR] fake"

[INFO] [task-api] task created title=Milk
[ERROR] fake
[INFO] [task-api] task created title=[REDACTED]

questions.q: You write log.debug("request", { headers: request.headers }). What is the best advice?
questions.explain: Redaction knows secret names like authorization and cookie. Other headers can still carry personal data. Logging only the fields you need is the safest habit.
options: It is fully safe: redaction hides every header
authorization and cookie are redacted, but other headers may be personal; log only the headers you need
It is safe because debug lines are never stored
Headers can never contain secrets, so log all of them

questions.q: Which set of rules does the lesson give for logs in production?
questions.explain: The platform (Docker, Kubernetes, a cloud service) collects standard output and ships it to a log store, which reads JSON fields without guessing. Rotating files is the platform's job, not your app's. await logger.flush() waits until every entry is written.
options: Readable text lines, written to a file that the app rotates each day
One JSON object per line, written to standard output, and flush before the process exits
One JSON array with all entries, written when the process exits
Only error entries, written to the terminal

questions.q: The JSON formatter writes one line of JSON per entry. This transport parses it and prints three fields. What does it print?
questions.explain: In JSON the metadata is a real object, not key=value text. Redaction runs in both formats, so apiKey is hidden here too.
options: info task created {"taskId":7,"apiKey":"[REDACTED]"}
info task created {"taskId":7,"apiKey":"k-1"}
3 task created {"taskId":7,"apiKey":"[REDACTED]"}
info task created taskId=7 apiKey=[REDACTED]

questions.q: Levels are numbers inside the logger. What does this print?
questions.explain: The more serious the level, the smaller the number: FATAL is 0 and TRACE is 5. loggerLevelFromName("warn") turns the name into the same number as LoggerLevel.WARN.
options:
1 3 4
true

4 2 1
true

1 3 4
false

error info debug
true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: loud is not one of the six level names, so loggerLevelFromName throws an InvalidLoggerLevelError and "ok" is never printed.
options: InvalidLoggerLevelError - Invalid logger level: loud.
ok
InvalidLoggerLevelError - loud
Error - Invalid logger level: loud.

questions.q: Why should createAppLogger throw at start-up when LOG_LEVEL contains a typo like "loud"?
questions.explain: A bad setting that fails loudly at start-up is found in seconds. A bad setting that is silently ignored can hide every log line you needed for weeks.
options: To make the app start faster
You notice the mistake at once, instead of silently logging the wrong things for weeks
Because the logger cannot work without a level
So the client learns the correct level name

questions.q: createAppLogger(env = process.env) takes the environment as a parameter. Why?
questions.explain: With the environment as a parameter, a test calls createAppLogger({ LOG_LEVEL: "debug" }) and checks the result. The default process.env keeps real use simple.
options: Because process.env cannot be read inside a function
A test can pass a plain object instead of changing real environment variables
So each request can choose its own log level
It is required by createLogger

questions.q: What does await logger.flush() do?
questions.explain: Some transports write in the background. Before the process exits, flush so that the last entries, often the most important ones, are not lost.
options: It deletes all old log entries
It sets the level back to info
It waits until every pending entry has been written
It sends the logs to the client

questions.q: This transport counts entries per level name. What does it print?
questions.explain: The level check happens before any transport runs. With the default threshold info, the debug entry never reaches the transport.
options: Map(2) { 'info' => 2, 'error' => 1 }
Map(3) { 'info' => 2, 'debug' => 1, 'error' => 1 }
Map(2) { 'info' => 1, 'error' => 1 }
Map(3) { 'info' => 1, 'debug' => 1, 'error' => 1 }

questions.q: Write a transport that counts entries per level name (entry.levelName) in the counts Map. The program should print Map(2) { 'warn' => 2, 'info' => 1 }.
questions.explain: Read the old count with counts.get(...) ?? 0 and store it plus one. The debug entry never reaches the transport, because the default threshold is info.

questions.q: Tests often check what the code logged. Finish the options: set the logger's level so only warn and more serious entries are kept, and add a transport that pushes each entry's levelName into seen. The program should print [ 'warn', 'error' ].
questions.explain: Pass level: LoggerLevel.WARN to createLogger. The info entry is dropped before any transport runs, so only the warn and error entries reach seen.

questions.q: Create queueLogger, a child of logger with the name task-api.queue and the metadata { component: "queue" }. The program should print [INFO] [task-api.queue] job done version=0.2.0 component=queue jobId=5.
questions.explain: logger.child({ name, metadata }) shares the parent's formatter, transports and level, and adds its own name and metadata after the parent's version.

questions.q:
Finish handleRequest: build a scoped logger with logger.withContext(createLoggerContext({ requestId })), log "listing tasks" with { count }, then log "request done" with { status: 200 }. The program should print:

[INFO] [task-api] listing tasks requestId=req-1 count=2
[INFO] [task-api] request done requestId=req-1 status=200
questions.explain: Create the scoped logger once per request and use it for every line of that request. Both lines then carry the same requestId without you repeating it.
questions.expected:
[INFO] [task-api] listing tasks requestId=req-1 count=2
[INFO] [task-api] request done requestId=req-1 status=200

questions.q: Finish levelFromEnv: when env.LOG_LEVEL has text, trim it, lower-case it and turn it into a level with loggerLevelFromName; otherwise return LoggerLevel.INFO. The program should print 3 4 2.
questions.explain: An empty or missing value falls back to info (3). A set value is cleaned up and converted, so " WARN " becomes warn (2). A typo would throw, which is what you want at start-up.

questions.q:
Finish logFailure: use the error's statusCode when it is a BaseError, otherwise 500. Below 500, write logger.warn("request rejected", { status }); otherwise logError(logger, error, "request failed", { status }). The program should print:

warn 400
error 500
questions.explain: A ValidationError has status 400: the client's mistake, so a warning. An unknown error counts as 500: your failure, so an error entry with the error attached.

questions.q: The Task API also logs email and phone, which are personal data. Configure the logger so both are redacted. The program should print [INFO] [task-api] signup userId=ada email=[REDACTED] phone=[REDACTED] plan=free.
questions.explain: redact: { keys: [...] } adds your own names to the default list. Redaction happens before any formatter or transport sees the entry.

questions.q: This line leaks the token, because it is inside the message text. Rewrite issueToken so it logs the fixed message "token issued" with only { userId } as metadata, and no token at all. The program should print [INFO] [auth] token issued userId=ada.
questions.explain: Keep the message fixed and put harmless values in metadata. Redaction never looks inside message text, so the safest token log contains no token at all.

questions.q: Finish the transport: parse the JSON line in entry.formatted and print its levelName, logger and message fields, separated by spaces. The program should print error task-api save failed.
questions.explain: With the JSON formatter, the formatter's text (entry.formatted) is one line of JSON. JSON.parse turns it back into an object whose fields a log store can read directly.

questions.q: Finish messagesFor(records, userId): return the message of every record whose userId matches. The program should print [ 'task created', 'task completed' ].
questions.explain: Because each record has a named userId field, the search is an exact comparison. With free sentences you would have to guess every way a user's name could appear.
